ai.definition: Space elevators are theoretical structures designed to transport cargo and people from the Earth's surface directly into space without the need for rockets.
ai.howItWorks: A space elevator consists of a cable anchored at one end to the ground and extending upward, with a counterweight beyond geostationary orbit. A climber moves up and down the cable, carrying payloads into space or returning from space.
ai.problemSolved: Reduces launch costs by providing an alternative method for transporting goods and people to space, potentially more cost-effective than traditional rockets.
ai.manufacturing: Requires advanced materials with extreme strength-to-weight ratios, such as carbon nanotubes or graphene. Current materials do not yet meet the required specifications.
ai.buildProcess: Involves constructing a cable from Earth's surface to geostationary orbit (about 35,786 km), anchoring it at both ends, and deploying climbers along its length.
ai.costDrivers: High material costs due to the need for ultra-strong cables; technological challenges in manufacturing and deployment; and regulatory and safety concerns.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Currently at a very early stage of development, with significant research needed before practical implementation is possible.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations exist for space elevators as they are not yet in operational use. However, international agreements and standards would likely be required once the technology matures.
ai.risks: Technological risks related to material science, structural integrity, and climber operation; environmental risks from potential accidents or decommissioning of the structure.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current lack of practical implementation. If developed, could significantly reduce launch costs, potentially leading to increased profitability in space-related industries.
ai.futureDevelopment: Continued research into material science and structural engineering is necessary for practical implementation. Potential breakthroughs in materials technology could accelerate development.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking required for carbon nanotube production.

glossary.def: An orbit around the Earth where an object remains above a fixed point on the equator, completing one revolution in 24 hours.
A vehicle that travels up and down a space elevator cable to transport cargo or people.

subsystems.name: Cable / ribbon
subsystems.role: the load-bearing ribbon that reaches from the equator out past geostationary orbit, roughly 36,000 km up.
parts: protective coating against atomic oxygen and debris

subsystems.name: Base anchor
subsystems.role: holds the bottom of the ribbon at a fixed equatorial point.

subsystems.name: Counterweight
subsystems.role: a mass beyond geostationary orbit that keeps the ribbon taut through centrifugal and gravitational balance.

subsystems.name: Climber
subsystems.role: robotic carrier that ascends the ribbon with payload.

subsystems.name: Power delivery
subsystems.role: supplies energy to climbers without heavy onboard fuel.

subsystems.name: Orbital station
subsystems.role: receives payloads near geostationary orbit and dispatches them to other orbits.

buildSteps.title: Make the material
buildSteps.detail: Draw or grow carbon-nanotube or graphene ribbons with the required strength-to-weight ratio, kilometres long and defect-free — the step that does not yet exist at any useful scale.

buildSteps.title: Deploy a seed ribbon
buildSteps.detail: A small initial ribbon is lowered from geostationary orbit toward Earth while a counterweight is raised outward, using gravity-gradient forces to keep it taut.

buildSteps.title: Anchor the base
buildSteps.detail: The lower end is captured and secured to a floating equatorial platform, which also manages tension and lightning risk.

buildSteps.title: Attach the counterweight
buildSteps.detail: A mass beyond geostationary orbit is secured to the upper end, or the ribbon is extended further so its own length acts as the counterweight.

buildSteps.title: Build up the ribbon
buildSteps.detail: Additional ribbons are added alongside the seed to increase load capacity, or the seed is reinforced, gradually forming a full tapered cable.

buildSteps.title: Test climbers
buildSteps.detail: Robotic climbers ascend the ribbon, powered by beamed energy, carrying small payloads to verify grip, speed and safety.

buildSteps.title: Scale to operation
buildSteps.detail: Multiple parallel ribbons or a larger cable support regular ascent of payloads to geostationary orbit and beyond, with traffic control and debris avoidance.

prerequisites.tech: Macroscopic carbon nanotube or graphene fibres
prerequisites.why: they exist only at laboratory scale and fall far short of the strength-to-weight ratio needed for a ribbon thousands of kilometres long.
the ribbon would likely have to be made in orbit to avoid its own weight; current in-space assembly is limited to small structures.
lasers and microwave links exist, but delivering megawatts to a moving climber over thousands of kilometres is untested.
a ribbon thousands of kilometres long is extremely vulnerable to impacts that could sever it.
satellites operate there routinely, providing the orbital node for the elevator.

pathway.milestone: laboratory research on ultra-strong carbon nanotube and graphene fibres, plus design studies of space elevator systems
pathway.unlocks: understanding of the material and structural challenges.

pathway.milestone: a proposed lunar space elevator, which could be built with existing high-strength fibres because the Moon's gravity is far weaker
pathway.unlocks: experience in tether deployment, anchoring and climbing.

pathway.milestone: a sub-scale Earth elevator or a ribbon in low Earth orbit tested with climbers
pathway.unlocks: proof of beamed power and long-term survival in the space environment.
low-cost, high-volume access to space and orbital solar power.
